video_title: Navigating the AI Reckoning with RBC Capital's Software Equity Research Team
gist: Dan Nathan sits down with RBC Capital's software analysts (Rishi, Matt Hedberg, Matt Swanson) ahead of RBC's TMT conference: software has lost its role as the 'anti-AI trade' and now sells off in lockstep with Nvidia-driven tech weakness, but the team argues the 'SaaS apocalypse' fears were overdone (Microsoft's recovery, AI-native companies still buying incumbent software) and that 2027's key catalyst is forward-looking AI metrics (ServiceNow AI ACV, Dynatrace consumption, Okta agent identity) finally showing up in P&L growth, with ad tech shifting toward SSPs, CTV and in-app formats.

themes.theme: Software sentiment: no longer the anti-AI hedge

insights.claim: Application software previously traded as the 'anti-AI trade' (rallying when AI infrastructure sold off), but fears that AI/Nvidia weakness has broader economic implications now have software moving in lockstep with the rest of tech.
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Software no longer offers a hedge against AI-infrastructure drawdowns; expect correlated tech selloffs until certainty returns.
insights.quote: you had a period of time in which software was especially application software was used as the anti-AII trade

insights.claim: Over the past year investors have paid up for certainty in software; when the 'floor of certainty' is removed, stocks can keep falling with no obvious bottom.
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Favor names with visible, simple stories; avoid ones where the narrative floor is in question.
insights.quote: when you start to remove the floor of certainty these stocks can just keep going down and down

insights.claim: In the current tape investors want simple stories that need no explaining: Cloudflare's huge quarter and guide was rewarded, while complex stories or deal push-outs (IBM, Dynatrace) were punished.
insights.speaker: Matt Hedberg (RBC, security/infrastructure software)
insights.so_what: Complexity carries a valuation penalty right now; simple beat-and-raise AI beneficiaries keep getting crowded into.
insights.quote: Investors want simple. They don't want complex.

insights.claim: Despite the 'SaaS apocalypse' rhetoric, CIOs repeatedly tell RBC that much AI spending is net-new rather than cannibalizing software budgets, so unused software budget plus pre-buying of AI budget and tokens could create an unusually large Q4 budget flush ('double whammy').
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Watch Q4 software prints for budget-flush upside; RBC's 2027 CIO survey is the data point to track.
insights.quote: a lot of the AI spending is actually net new it's not coming out of software budgets

insights.claim: Many software companies are stuck in 'no man's land', trading at all-time-low multiples of roughly 8-9x cash flow, where margin expansion no longer rescues the stock, raising the question of reinvesting for growth durability instead.
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Cheap-on-cash-flow software is not a catalyst by itself; look for names that prove durable growth as AI mix rises.
insights.quote: You have some of these companies trading at all-time low multiples at you know eight times nine times cash flow but margin expansion doesn't save the stock

insights.claim: Dan Nathan expects 2026 not to be a 20%+ Nasdaq year (index roughly up 9%, S&P similar) and frames the environment as one for finding unusual long-side values while avoiding big pitfalls.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Stock-picking/dispersion environment rather than broad beta.

themes.theme: Microsoft's rebound and the Copilot leg

insights.claim: Investors got Microsoft wrong on three counts at peak SaaS-apocalypse fear: the 'vibe code your own Excel' threat, the idea Azure was losing the hyperscale cloud war (it was just disciplined on capex and stayed cash-flow positive while peers burned cash and tapped markets), and the view that Office Copilot had failed.
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Microsoft's earlier 30%+ drawdown was narrative-driven; capex discipline is a differentiator vs. cash-burning hyperscalers.
insights.quote: we're just going to vibe code our own Excel, which is a terrible idea

insights.claim: Office Copilot is turning: engagement metrics and net paid adds are improving, the Office line has already accelerated, and customer feedback is meaningfully better than a year ago after Satya Nadella stepped back into the product.
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Copilot ARPU uplift on roughly half a billion paid Office users is the next leg of the Microsoft story beyond Azure.
insights.quote: customer feedback to office co-pilot is meaningfully better than it was even a year ago

insights.claim: Microsoft's early decision to build Copilot model-agnostic (usable with any LLM, including open-weight models) lets it orchestrate multiple models simultaneously; model orchestration - picking the right model for the right job cost-efficiently - is a key bull case for Microsoft and other incumbents.
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Reduced OpenAI dependence lowers model-cost and vendor risk; orchestration becomes an incumbent moat.
insights.quote: this is a really important bullcase for Microsoft and others is that model orchestration piece

insights.claim: Cloud growth has reaccelerated across hyperscalers: Azure roughly high-30s/40% year-over-year, GCP around 100% off a smaller base, and AWS reaccelerating after bottoming around 12-13%.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Validates AI demand at the infrastructure layer for all three hyperscalers.

insights.claim: Microsoft likely stays a defensive holding into 2027 given its duration; the baton would pass away from it only when investors see live, non-custom-built knowledge-worker AI use cases, shifting focus from AI infrastructure (where cracks are already appearing) to applications.
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Watch for packaged knowledge-worker AI adoption as the signal to rotate from Microsoft to app names.
insights.quote: we're already starting to see a little bit of cracks in that trade

themes.theme: Incumbent SaaS defenses: data moats, FDEs, frontier-lab partnerships

insights.claim: ServiceNow looks cheap on 2027 estimates, but investors debate whether the market is discounting an organic growth deceleration; its acquisitions (including cyber assets) are about broadening its data estate as a defense against TAM encroachment.
insights.speaker: Matt Hedberg (RBC, security/infrastructure software)
insights.so_what: ServiceNow re-rates only if growth proves durable; acquisitions are defensive data-moat building.
insights.quote: part of the defense mechanisms to prevent maybe TAM encroachment is to just get bigger data estates

insights.claim: Enterprise software vendors are adding cyber capabilities (ServiceNow cyber acquisitions, Workday buying an identity vendor) because customers deploying these platforms need security alongside, so expect more cross-pollination and consolidation, with Salesforce also acquisitive.
insights.speaker: Matt Hedberg (RBC, security/infrastructure software)
insights.so_what: Pure-play cyber vendors face new platform competitors; M&A in identity/security likely continues.

insights.claim: The rise of forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) at ServiceNow and others signals vendors must push harder to get IT-constrained customers to deploy more AI beyond the already-converted base; if it translates to durable growth the stock could become interesting.
insights.speaker: Matt Hedberg (RBC, security/infrastructure software)
insights.so_what: Treat FDE build-outs as both a demand-friction warning and a potential durability catalyst.

insights.claim: Every technology wave needs handholding: at their peaks Workday was ~35% professional services, ServiceNow ~30% (now under 5%) and Veeva ~45%; FDEs are today's version, aimed at the 'enterprise AI ROI paradox' where spending is high but tangible savings are unproven.
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Rising services mix in AI rollouts is a normal early-cycle phase, not necessarily a margin red flag.
insights.quote: there's still this paradox of enterprise AI ROI

insights.claim: Explicit partnerships with frontier labs (e.g., Salesforce at Dreamforce, Benioff appearing with Dario Amodei) dampen the 'AI labs will destroy Salesforce' narrative and reflect co-opetition; incumbents must stay open to whichever AI model customers want and monetize over time.
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Lab partnerships can put a sentiment floor under SaaS names.

insights.claim: High-growth AI-native companies hitting $100M-$500M ARR actually run on incumbent software with no plans to replace it; the full cost of building, scaling, supporting and securing a homegrown stack becomes prohibitive, so 'AI natives will replace SaaS' is largely a false narrative.
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Undercuts the core SaaS-apocalypse disruption thesis; supports incumbent application vendors.
insights.quote: they're actually using a lot of these incumbent software solutions with no plans to replace them anytime soon

insights.claim: Enterprises trying to maximize token and AI budgets are increasingly delegating model selection and token optimization to incumbent vendors like Salesforce, ServiceNow, Workday and Microsoft.
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Incumbents can capture AI budget as orchestration layers.

themes.theme: Cyber, infrastructure and the non-human traffic thesis

insights.claim: Cyber names rallied hard off the early-May lows (Okta, Palo Alto, CrowdStrike, Cloudflare); pre-3Q investors tried rotating into tier-2 AI beneficiaries but those benefits didn't manifest, sending money back to tier-1 AI winners, whose moves are now mainly a valuation issue.
insights.speaker: Matt Hedberg (RBC, security/infrastructure software)
insights.so_what: Tier-1 AI winners in cyber remain crowded and not cheap relative to broad software.

insights.claim: As AI models get smarter there will be more and more software vulnerabilities (e.g., the recent PHP vulnerability), keeping security spending tied to AI rollouts and fundamentals at the big cyber consolidators very strong.
insights.speaker: Matt Hedberg (RBC, security/infrastructure software)
insights.so_what: AI adoption is a structural tailwind for cyber platform consolidators.
insights.quote: as these AI models get smarter there's going to be more and more of these vulnerabilities

insights.claim: Cloudflare's Matthew Prince believes non-human (bot/agent) internet traffic will grow 1,000x within five years; Cloudflare said on its Q2 call non-human traffic already equals human traffic, with profound implications for cyber, token use, application software and advertising.
insights.speaker: Matt Hedberg (RBC, security/infrastructure software)
insights.so_what: Positions identity, edge/network and bot-management vendors as long-run beneficiaries; challenges ad models.
insights.quote: he believes with within the next five years non-human traffic will 1,000x from here

insights.claim: Okta is accelerating growth without any contribution yet from agentic capabilities; RBC sees it well positioned for the 1,000x growth in non-human traffic because understanding what agents are doing (agent identity) is critical.
insights.speaker: Matt Hedberg (RBC, security/infrastructure software)
insights.so_what: Okta has agentic upside not yet in numbers; a 2027 watch name.
insights.quote: they're accelerating growth, but interestingly, none of it's because of agentic capabilities

insights.claim: The key 2027 delta for infrastructure/cyber software is whether forward-looking AI metrics (ServiceNow AI ACV records, Dynatrace consumption growth) convert to P&L revenue acceleration; until then investors will keep crowding tier-1 AI winners such as Datadog, Cloudflare, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto and Snowflake.
insights.speaker: Matt Hedberg (RBC, security/infrastructure software)
insights.so_what: Okta, ServiceNow and Dynatrace are the names to watch for proof; expect multiple quarters of skepticism.
insights.quote: when will those forward-looking metrics actually translate to improve P&L growth

insights.claim: The waterfall of AI monetization into application software is the 2027 switch-flip: investors have left most app names for dead over seat-based pricing fears, but vendors that innovated at the AI layer will show real monetization and growth inflection.
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Contrarian long setup in beaten-down application software for 2027.
insights.quote: I think it's the waterfall of AI monetization going to application software

themes.theme: Ad tech in an agentic, zero-click world

insights.claim: Generative AI is shifting software toward outcome- and consumption-based pricing, which flips the old view of consumption-driven ad tech as lower quality (vs. SaaS ARR/cRPO visibility); performance ad platforms like Zeta, AppLovin and Liftoff win because they show a clear dollar-in, $1.20-out ROI.
insights.speaker: Matt Swanson (RBC, ad tech/IBM)
insights.so_what: Performance-ad businesses may deserve multiple re-rating as outcome pricing becomes the norm.
insights.quote: you put a dollar in the this machine and gives you a$120 out

insights.claim: AppLovin's Q2 was its first revenue miss in history, sparking a 'false narrative of thesis risk' (TAM too small/fully captured) among new investors; Q3 then delivered the best beat and raise in its history, with the stock moving roughly 700 to 250 and back to 400.
insights.speaker: Matt Swanson (RBC, ad tech/IBM)
insights.so_what: Single-datapoint thesis scares in high-multiple names can create entry points; Dan Nathan is skeptical of the bounce.
insights.quote: feels like a false narrative of thesis risk

insights.claim: Light Google search and Amazon advertising versus consensus make it hard for investors to see open-internet ad tech (Magnite, The Trade Desk) outperforming, and bots/agents are very hard to monetize with ads.
insights.speaker: Matt Swanson (RBC, ad tech/IBM)
insights.so_what: Walled-garden softness is a read-through negative for open-web ad tech.
insights.quote: Really hard to monetize from an advertisement to a robot

insights.claim: Ad tech winners will be those with exposure to attention- and viewability-maximizing formats (CTV, mobile in-app, podcasts) and those who own the data and audience targeting as agentic buying grows.
insights.speaker: Matt Swanson (RBC, ad tech/IBM)
insights.so_what: Screen ad-tech names by format exposure and first-party data ownership.

insights.claim: If generative AI changes how product searches start, Amazon's sponsored-search ad business is threatened; this is driving renewed brand spend (so shoppers start searches with a brand) and 'performance prompting' on CTV and in-app to create unplanned purchase moments upstream of search.
insights.speaker: Matt Swanson (RBC, ad tech/IBM)
insights.so_what: Budgets shift toward brand and shoppable CTV; risk to search-based ad models.
insights.quote: what if that is no longer the way people start that search?

insights.claim: Supply-side platforms PubMatic and Magnite are both up a bit over 80% this year as agentic buying and more fragmented buyers give SSPs (historically seen as secondary to DSPs like The Trade Desk) more credit; server-side, publisher-close targeting with logged-in data is the emerging theme.
insights.speaker: Matt Swanson (RBC, ad tech/IBM)
insights.so_what: SSPs are shedding the commodity label; sentiment improving relative to DSPs.

insights.claim: IBM worked in 2025 as a way to play generative AI without picking winners (infrastructure, consulting, Granite LLMs, governance, quantum, Confluent/HashiCorp), but its Q2 preannouncement on server deals pushed out (as customers reprioritized capex and pulled memory/storage deals forward) hit the core thesis.
insights.speaker: Matt Swanson (RBC, ad tech/IBM)
insights.so_what: IBM's mainframe durability question, not its AI themes, now drives the stock.

insights.claim: IBM's Q3 was more well-rounded (capex better, software outperforming, consulting green shoots), but the Q4 deal cycle looks more like Q2, so the stock hinges on whether investors accept management's claim that server push-outs are value-preserving rather than value-destroying.
insights.speaker: Matt Swanson (RBC, ad tech/IBM)
insights.so_what: Q4 infrastructure results are the swing factor for IBM.

insights.claim: RBC's internal AI tool (Aiden) is used daily by the team with rising token bills; Rishi says AI cut the time between two deep-dive thematic reports (physical AI, AI in healthcare) from about three months to 10 days.
insights.speaker: Rishi (RBC software analyst)
insights.so_what: Evidence of real knowledge-worker productivity gains and growing enterprise token spend at financial firms.
insights.quote: this would have been three months between these, not 10 days

insights.claim: In a class of 25 college seniors, none were using AI agents for job searches and some young people had never heard of Meta's Muse agent, leaving Dan Nathan unsure whether consumer agents become 'the metaverse' or take off; Muse numbers in Meta's report were not exciting.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Consumer agent adoption may lag hype; a risk to consumer-AI monetization narratives.
insights.quote: So either agents are going to be like the metaverse for consumers

insights.claim: Dan Nathan views smartphone hardware as table stakes with AI as the differentiator, sees Gemini embedded across Android as a Google strength, and calls Apple's strength a head-scratcher since it has not yet shown an on-device/small-model AI edge.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Skepticism on Apple's AI positioning versus Google.
insights.quote: an Apple to me is just a head scratcher
